title: States and Transitions
question: Deterministic, nondeterministic, and probabilistic rules look different. What do they have in common?

title: What can we know about one bit?
rows: A fair coin set the bit
takeaway: Every kind of knowledge takes one form: a weight for each configuration, written \(v_0\ket0+v_1\ket1\).
notes: A configuration is what the register holds; the state is what we know about it. All three kinds of knowledge assign a number to each configuration.
The kets are bookkeeping for now: terms for the same configuration add, terms for different configurations stay apart. The weights mean different things in different rows.

title: How do we write one step?
label: Notation
statement: \(\bra jS\ket i\) is the weight of the arrow from \(i\) to \(j\) under the step \(S\).
note: Read right to left: start at \(i\), apply \(S\), arrive at \(j\). For NOT: \(\bra1X\ket0=\bra0X\ket1=1\) and \(\bra0X\ket0=\bra1X\ket1=0\).
notes: A state diagram has one circle per configuration and one arrow for each permitted transition. A missing arrow has weight zero.

title: How do we see a whole run?
lead: Copy the configurations once for each time and join the copies by the arrows of the rule.
takeaway: A run is a path through the time-expanded diagram. From 0, NOT gives 0, 1, 0.
notes: The left panel is the state diagram of NOT; the right panel repeats the configurations at t = 0, 1, 2.

title: Can a deterministic run be traced backward?
takeaway: Both rules fix the next step. Only NOT fixes the previous one: two arrows enter 0 under RESET, so it is not reversible.
notes: Both rules are deterministic: one arrow leaves each configuration, so the start fixes the run and a definite state stays definite.
A deterministic rule with exactly one arrow entering each configuration is reversible.

title: What if a configuration has several successors?
lead: KEEP-OR-FLIP permits both successors from either bit: four two-step paths from 0.
takeaway: A configuration is reachable if at least one permitted path ends there. This is possibility, not probability.
notes: Nondeterministic acceptance has the same form: an input is accepted if some permitted run accepts.
Counting paths does not make an endpoint more likely; the rule says nothing about likelihood.

title: What does a probabilistic rule add?
lead: COIN gives every arrow the probability \(P(j\mid i)=\tfrac12\).
takeaway: Two exclusive histories end at 0, so \(P(c_2=0)=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\).
notes: The weights leaving each configuration add to one. We assume the configuration holds everything needed to predict the next step (the Markov assumption).
Unlike a deterministic rule, COIN does not fix one run; unlike a nondeterministic rule, it predicts how often each outcome occurs.

title: Sum and Product Rules
question: Once arrows carry weights, how do we compute the weight of an endpoint?

title: What is one path worth?
steps: A path \(i\to j\to k\) needs every arrow along it.
Its weight is the product \(\bra kT\ket j\,\bra jS\ket i\), with the first step on the right.
Allowed arrow 1, missing arrow 0: the product is 1 exactly when the whole path is permitted.
For COIN, each two-step path has weight \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14\).
takeaway: Product rule: multiply along a path.
notes: For probabilities the factors are conditional probabilities of successive steps; they need not be independent events.

title: How do paths to one endpoint combine?
steps: \[\bra kTS\ket i=\sum_j\bra kT\ket j\,\bra jS\ket i\]
Deterministic: one path. Nondeterministic: the sum counts paths. Probabilistic: the endpoint probability.
COIN: \(\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12\) at either endpoint.
Every contribution is nonnegative, so adding a path can never lower a total.
takeaway: Sum rule: add across paths. With nonnegative weights, nothing ever cancels.
notes: The left side treats the two steps as one combined step TS: first S, then T.

title: How does a whole state change in one step?
steps: \[v^\prime_j=\sum_i\bra jS\ket i\,v_i\]
Each configuration goes to its weighted successors: \(S\ket i=\sum_j\bra jS\ket i\,\ket j\).
Example: \(\mathrm{COIN}\ket0=\tfrac12\ket0+\tfrac12\ket1\).
A reversible rule only permutes configurations: \(\mathrm{CNOT}\ket{10}=\ket{11}\). RESET and COIN merge distinct states.
notes: The state carries everything needed to predict the next step, without a list of earlier paths.

title: Signed Weights
question: What changes if a weight may be negative?

title: What does a negative arrow do to a path?
steps: The product rule is unchanged: \(\bra kS\ket j\,\bra jS\ket i\).
An odd number of negative arrows makes the path weight negative.
\((\tfrac12)(-\tfrac12)=-\tfrac14,\qquad(-\tfrac12)(-\tfrac12)=+\tfrac14\)
A negative path weight is not a negative probability. It is a signed contribution to a later sum.
notes: This is a mathematical extension of the path description; its physical meaning comes later.

title: Can two paths add up to nothing?
lead: Two routes contribute \(ca\) and \(db\), with \(a=b=c=\tfrac12\) and \(d=-\tfrac12\).
takeaway: \(\tfrac14-\tfrac14=0\): cancellation. Adding a path can now lower a total.
notes: Only contributions to the same final configuration add. A weight +1/4 at 0 and −1/4 at 1 stay separate.

title: Can a step spread a bit out and still undo itself?
question: Give three arrows the weight \(c\) and one arrow the weight \(-c\). Apply the step twice, starting from 0. What must \(c\) be to return to 0 with weight 1?
hint: Count the two paths into 0 and the two paths into 1.
answer: Into 0: \(c^2+c^2=2c^2\). Into 1: \(c^2-c^2=0\). So \(2c^2=1\) and \(c=1/\sqrt2\). This step is the Hadamard step \(H\).
notes: The negative arrow is the arrow from 1 to 1. Starting from 1 gives the other check: the paths to 0 cancel and the paths to 1 reinforce.

title: The Hadamard step undoes itself
takeaway: \(HH=I\). After one step the squared weights add to one, \(c^2+c^2=1\): a hint that squares will give probabilities.
notes: Replace the negative arrow by a positive one and both inputs give the same intermediate weights; the second step can no longer recover the start. Cancellation is what makes the step reversible.

title: Complex Amplitudes and Interference
question: A sign is a two-way choice. What does a continuously varying direction allow?

title: Is there a square root of NOT?
question: Find a step \(\sqrt X\), with stay-weight \(a\) and switch-weight \(b\), such that two steps of it give NOT.
hint: Two steps: the return paths give \(a^2+b^2\); the switch paths give \(2ab\).
answer: We need \(a^2+b^2=0\) and \(2ab=1\). No real numbers work. Complex numbers do: \(a=\tfrac{1+i}{2},\ b=\tfrac{1-i}{2}\).
notes: Neither deterministic reversible step on one bit squares to NOT: the identity and NOT both square to the identity.

title: Squares that cancel
lead: In the plane, multiplying by \(i\) is a quarter turn, so \(i^2=-1\).
takeaway: \(a^2=\tfrac i2\) and \(b^2=-\tfrac i2\): the return paths cancel, and \(2ab=1\) sends the bit across.
notes: Weights that may be complex are called amplitudes. They obey the same sum and product rules.

title: Which probability rule fits complex amplitudes?
steps: \(a^2=i/2\) cannot be a probability.
Use the squared magnitude instead: \(p(j)=v_jv_j^*=|v_j|^2\).
Normalization: \(\sum_j|v_j|^2=1\).
Add amplitudes first, then square: \(|A+B|^2=|A|^2+|B|^2+AB^*+A^*B\).
To keep total probability one, each step needs unit-length, mutually orthogonal columns.
notes: The cross terms are what distinguish adding amplitudes from adding probabilities. Two steps of √X: return contributions i/2 and −i/2 sum to zero.
Write a unit arrow at angle φ as e^{iφ} = cos φ + i sin φ; multiplying amplitudes adds their phases.

title: How does a phase change an outcome?
steps: Start from \((\ket0+e^{i\phi}\ket1)/\sqrt2\): probabilities \(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\) for every \(\phi\).
\[p(0)\text{ after }H=\left|\frac{1+e^{i\phi}}{2}\right|^2=\frac{1+\cos\phi}{2}\]
\(\phi=0\): certainly 0. \(\phi=\pi\): certainly 1. \(\phi=\pi/2\): even odds.
A common (global) phase changes nothing; a relative phase changes what happens next.
takeaway: Interference: amplitudes add at a common endpoint before we square.
notes: Z multiplies the amplitude at 1 by −1, a relative phase of π. Inserted between two Hadamard steps it turns a certain 0 into a certain 1.

title: Does a record of the path matter?
lead: Run \(H\), then CNOT onto a record bit, then \(H\) again.

right.label: Record undone
items: Apply CNOT again before the last H.
Both contributions now reach 10, and cancel.
The run returns to \(\ket{00}\) with certainty.

takeaway: Anything that can tell the paths apart belongs in the configuration. Uncomputing the record restores interference.
notes: Ignoring the record does not merge its two values into one configuration; the loss of interference follows from the different endpoints whether or not anyone reads the record.

title: What we found
items: A state is a weight per configuration; a step is a weight per arrow.
Multiply along paths, add across paths, for every kind of rule.
Signed weights cancel, which lets the Hadamard step undo itself.
Complex amplitudes give a square root of NOT; probabilities are squared magnitudes.
Paths interfere only where they meet; a record of the path prevents it.
